nameStory: This tiny crab gets its name from its unusual lifestyle choice — it lives inside the tubes built by marine worms, particularly chaetopterid worms (marine bristle worms). The 'pea' part refers to its small, rounded size, about as big as a garden pea. It's essentially a tiny roommate that moves into someone else's home!
description: The tube pea crab is a miniature crab that lives as a guest inside the tubes of marine worms along New England's coast. These crabs are incredibly small, typically less than half an inch across, with a soft, rounded shell that's often pale pink or whitish. The females are larger and softer than males, with a body perfectly adapted for squeezing through narrow tube openings. They spend their entire adult lives inside their worm host's tube, filter-feeding on particles in the water.

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Extremely small crab, less than half an inch across, with a soft, rounded carapace that feels almost squishy compared to typical hard-shelled crabs

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale pink, whitish, or translucent appearance that allows you to see internal organs through the thin shell

idTips.label: Location found
idTips.description: Always discovered inside tube-dwelling marine worm burrows, never free-living on rocks or sand

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Carapace feels soft and flexible rather than hard and rigid like most crabs, with a smooth surface

idTips.label: Body proportions
idTips.description: Females noticeably larger and rounder than males, with a broad, swollen abdomen for carrying eggs

habitat: Found in intertidal and shallow subtidal zones along New England's rocky and muddy shores, specifically inside the tubes of marine bristle worms like the parchment tube worm. Look for them in protected bays, estuaries, and tide pools where their worm hosts build U-shaped or straight tubes in the sediment. They're most commonly discovered when examining worm tubes during low tide explorations.

seasonality.spring: Adult crabs become more active as water temperatures rise, with mating season beginning. Look for egg-bearing females inside worm tubes during tide pool exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when crabs are most likely to be found. Females carry bright orange egg masses that are visible through their translucent shells during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding and growing before winter dormancy. Young crabs may be settling into new host tubes during this period.
seasonality.winter: Crabs remain inside host tubes in a less active state. They can still be found but are sluggish and less responsive to disturbance.

funFact: Female tube pea crabs can actually outlive their worm hosts and will sometimes move to a new tube when their original roommate dies — they're like the ultimate apartment hoppers of the marine world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small pea crabs found in New England, but the tube pea crab is the only one that lives exclusively inside worm tubes rather than with mollusks like oysters or mussels. If you find a tiny crab inside a clam or oyster, it's a different pea crab species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pea crabs,' these aren't closely related to garden peas at all — the name simply refers to their small, round size. The relationship with their worm hosts appears to be commensal, meaning the crab benefits while the worm is neither helped nor harmed.
compareHints: Since this is the only Tubicolixa species in New England waters, compare it to other pea crabs in the Pinnotheridae family. Unlike oyster pea crabs which live in mollusk shells, tube pea crabs are found exclusively in worm tubes. They're also smaller and softer-bodied than most other regional pea crab species, with a more translucent appearance that distinguishes them from their relatives.
